name: Pet services business
blurb: Walk, sit, board or groom other people's pets, paid per visit, walk or groom
title: Dog Walking, Pet Sitting and Grooming Business: How to Start
description: How a dog walking, pet sitting or dog grooming business makes money, what you need, licences and insurance to check, the risks and how to test it first.
h1: How to start a dog walking, pet sitting or grooming business
answer: A pet services business looks after other people's animals: dog walking, pet sitting or home visits, boarding, and dog grooming. Walking and sitting can start with almost no equipment, while grooming needs training, tools and a suitable space or van. The catches are responsibility for animals that can be hurt or lost, licences for boarding in some places, and a calendar that fills and empties with school holidays.

body: Dog walkers charge per walk, often with group walks earning more per hour than solo walks. Pet sitters charge per visit or per night; groomers charge per groom, priced by breed, size and coat condition. Regular weekly clients are the base; holiday sitting and boarding add busy peaks.
Margin goes to travel between homes, insurance, platform commission if you get bookings through an app, grooming products and equipment, and time lost to cancellations.

ul: For walking and sitting: leads, waste bags, treats, a first-aid kit for pets and a way to keep keys secure.
For grooming: training, clippers, dryers, a grooming table and a room, salon or van with water and drainage.
Insurance that covers care, custody and control of animals, plus liability if a dog injures someone.

Local paperwork: rules differ by country and city. For example, in England home boarding for dogs and dog day care need an animal activity licence from the local council; some places also have rules for commercial dog walking, so check with your local council or city.
Written terms: emergency contacts, vet details, vaccination requirements and what happens if a pet is ill or aggressive.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: Anyone with pet allergies or a fear of large dogs
People happy to walk in all weather
People who want weekends and holidays off
Groomers with patience and steady hands
Anyone unwilling to train before charging for grooming

ul: A lost, injured or sick animal in your care is the biggest risk, both for the pet and your reputation. Use secure leads, check gates and know the nearest emergency vet.
Dog bites and dog fights in group walks; meet each dog first and refuse ones you cannot handle.
Platform dependence: apps bring bookings but take commission and can change rules or remove your profile.
Seasonality: holiday periods are packed and other weeks can be quiet.
Grooming brings physical strain on back and wrists, plus the risk of cuts and nicks to animals.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Walk or sit for three friends' or neighbours' pets for a few weeks at a real price.
Check map listings and pet-care apps to see how many walkers, sitters or groomers serve your area.
Ask local vets, pet shops and dog parks where owners find help today.
For grooming, take a short course and practise on willing friends' dogs before charging.
Count enquiries from one post in a local community group over two weeks.
Register the business, get pet-care insurance and check any licence for boarding or day care.
Choose one service to start, such as solo walks or home visits, and price it clearly.
Prepare a client form with vet details, vaccinations, behaviour notes and emergency consent.
Hold a meet-and-greet with every new pet before the first booking.
Ask satisfied owners for reviews and introductions to their neighbours.

faq.q: Do I need a licence to be a dog walker or pet sitter?
faq.a: In many places, simple walking or sitting in the owner's home needs no special licence beyond normal business registration, but boarding or day care often does. In England, for example, home boarding and dog day care need a council licence. Check local rules and any park or city limits on dog numbers.

faq.q: Should I use a pet-sitting app or find my own clients?
faq.a: Apps can bring your first bookings quickly, but they take a commission and own the relationship. Many sitters use them to start and move regular clients to direct bookings where the app's terms allow.

faq.q: How do I become a dog groomer?
faq.a: Take a recognised grooming course or train under an experienced groomer, then practise on a range of breeds. Grooming without training risks injuring animals and losing clients.
